source_text: Super quae omnia ipse continens cuncta, nihil extra ro se uacuum deserens, nulli deo superiori (ut quidam putant) locum reliquit. quandoquidem ipse uniuersa sinu perfectae magnitudinis et potestatis incluserit, intentus semper operi suo, et uadens per omnia, et mouens cuncta, et uiuificans uniuersa, et conspiciens tota, et in concordiam elementorum omnium discordantes materias sic conectens, ut ex disparibus elementis ita sit unus mundus ista coagmentata conspiratione solidatus, ut nulla ui dissolui possit, nisi cum illum solus ipse qui fecit, ad maiora alia praestanda nobis, solui iusserit. hunc enim legimus omnia continere: et ideo nihil extra ipsum esse potuisse; quippe cum originem omnino non habeat, consequenter nec exitum sentiat: nisi forte, quod absit, aliquando esse coeperit, nec super omnia sit, sed dum post aliquid esse coeperit, infra id sit quod ante ipsum fuerit, minor inuentus potestate, dum posterior denotatur etiam ipso tempore. ob hanc ergo causam semper immensus, quia nihil illo maius est; semper aeternus, quia nihil illo antiquius. id enim quod sine origine est, praecedi a nullo potest, dum non habet tempus. ideo immortalis, non deficiens in consummationis exitu. et quoniam sine lege est quicquid sine origine est, modum temporis excludit, dum se debitorem nemini sentit. De hoc ergo, ac de eis quae sunt ipsius et in eo sunt, nec mens hominis quae sint, quanta sint, et qualia sint, digne concipere potest, nec eloquentia sermonis humani aequabilem maiestati eius uirtutem expromit. ad cogitandam enim et ad eloquendam illius maiestatem et eloquentia omnis merito muta est, et mens omnis exigua est. maior est enim mente ipsa, nec cogitari possit quantus sit, ne si potuerit cogitari, mente humana minor sit, qua concipi possit. maior est quoque omni sermone, nec edici possit: ne si potuerit edici, humano sermone minor sit, quo, cum edicitur, et circumiri et colligi possit. quicquid enim de illo cogitatum fuerit, minus ipso erit: et quicquid enuntiatum fuerit, minus illo comparatum circum ipsum erit. sentire enim illum taciti aliquatenus possumus; ut autem ipse est, sermone explicare non possumus. siue enim illum dixeris lucem, creaturam ipsius magis quam ipsum dixeris; ipsum non expresseris: siue illum dixeris uirtutem, potentiam ipsius magis quam ipsum dixeris et deprompseris: siue dixeris maiestatem, honorem ipsius magis quam illum ipsum descripseris. et quid per singula quaeque percurrens longum facio? semel totum explicabo: quicquid omnino de illo rettuleris, rem aliquam ipsius magis et uirtutem, quam ipsum explicaueris. quid enim de eo condigne aut dicas, aut sentias, qui omnibus et sermonibus et sensibus maior est? nisi quod uno modo (et hoc ipsum quo modo possumus, quo modo capimus, quo modo intellegere licet?) quid sit deus mente capiemus, si cogitauerimus id illum esse, quod quale et quantum sit non possit intellegi, nec in ipsam quidem cogitationem possit uenire. nam si ad solis aspectum oculorum nostrorum acies hebescit, ne orbem ipsum obtutus inspiciat obuiorum sibi superatus fulgore radiorum, hoc idem mentis acies patitur in cogitatione omni de deo; et quanto ad considerandum deum plus intenditur, tanto magis ipsa cogitationis suae luce caecatur. quid enim de eo (ut iterum repetam) condigne dicas, qui est sublimitate omni sublimior, et altitudine omni altior, et profundo omni profundior, et omni luce lucidior, et omni claritate clarior, omni splendore splendidior, omni robore robustior, omni uirtute uirilior, omni pulchritudine pulchrior, ueritate omni uerior, et fortitudine omni fortior, et maiestate omni maior, et omni potentia potentior, et omnibus diuitiis ditior, omni prudentia prudentior, et omni benignitate benignior, omni bonitate melior, omni iustitia iustior, omni clementia clementior? minora enim sint necesse est omnium genera uirtutum eo ipso, qui uirtutum omnium et deus et parens est: ut uere dici possit id deus esse, quod eiusmodi est cui comparari nihil potest. super omne est enim quod dici potest. mens est enim quaedam gignens et complens omnia, quae sine ullo aut initio aut termino temporis causas rerum, naturaliter nexas ad utilitatem omnium summa et perfecta ratione moderetur.
pass_a_gloss: He himself, containing all things, leaving nothing outside of himself empty, has not left room for a superior God, as some think. Since he himself has enclosed all things in the bosom of perfect magnitude and power, always intent on his work, and going through all things, and moving all things, and giving life to all things, and seeing all things, and connecting in harmony the discordant materials of all elements, so that from different elements there is one world, solidified by this conspiracy, so that it cannot be dissolved by any force, unless he himself, who made it, orders it to be dissolved, so that he may give us greater things. For we read that he contains all things, and therefore nothing can be outside of him, since he does not have an origin, and consequently does not feel an end, unless perhaps, which is absurd, he has begun to exist at some point, and is not above all things, but is below what was before him, found to be less powerful, since he is also later in time. Therefore, he is always immense, because nothing is greater than him; always eternal, because nothing is older than him. For what is without origin cannot be preceded by anything, since it does not have time. Therefore, he is immortal, not failing in the end of consummation. And since what is without origin is without law, he excludes the measure of time, since he feels himself to be indebted to no one. Therefore, neither the human mind can conceive what he is, how great he is, and what kind he is, nor can human eloquence express a virtue equal to his majesty. For in contemplating and speaking of his majesty, all eloquence is rightly mute, and all mind is small. He is greater than the mind itself, and cannot be thought of as to how great he is, lest, if he could be thought of, he would be less than the human mind, by which he can be conceived. He is also greater than all speech, and cannot be expressed, lest, if he could be expressed, he would be less than human speech, by which, when he is expressed, he can be encompassed and collected. For whatever is thought of him is less than he is, and whatever is spoken of him is less than he is, when compared to him. We can sense him in silence to some extent, but we cannot explain him in speech, as he is. For if you call him light, you have said a creature of his, rather than him; if you call him virtue, you have said his power, rather than him; if you call him majesty, you have said his honor, rather than him. And why do I make a long discussion, going through each thing individually? I will explain the whole thing once: whatever you say of him, you have explained something of his, and his virtue, rather than him. For what can you say or think of him worthily, who is greater than all speeches and senses? Unless, in one way, we can grasp what God is with our mind, if we think that he is what cannot be understood as to what kind and how great he is, and cannot even come into thought. For if the vision of our eyes is dulled by the sight of the sun, so that it cannot look at the orb itself, overcome by the brilliance of the rays, the same thing happens to the vision of the mind in all thought of God, and the more it is directed to consider God, the more it is blinded by the light of its own thought. For what can you say worthily of him, who is more sublime than all sublimity, and higher than all height, and deeper than all depth, and more lucid than all light, and more clear than all clarity, more splendid than all splendor, more robust than all robustness, more virile than all virtue, more beautiful than all beauty, more true than all truth, more strong than all strength, more majestic than all majesty, more powerful than all power, richer than all riches, more prudent than all prudence, more benign than all benignity, better than all goodness, more just than all justice, more merciful than all mercy? For all kinds of virtues must be less than him, who is the God and parent of all virtues, so that it can be truly said that he is God, who is such that nothing can be compared to him. He is above all that can be said, for he is a certain mind that generates and fills all things, which, without any beginning or end of time, naturally and with perfect reason, moderates the causes of things, connected to the utility of all things.

pass_b_english: Containing all things within himself, he leaves nothing empty outside his being, so he has not left room for a superior God, as some imagine. Indeed, he has enclosed the whole universe in the embrace of his perfect magnitude and power. He is ever intent on his work, passing through all things, moving all things, giving life to all things, and seeing all things. He joins the discordant materials of every element into harmony, so that from differing elements one world arises, solidified by this conspiracy, which no force can dissolve unless he who made it commands it to be dissolved, so that he may give us greater things. We read that he contains all things; therefore nothing can exist outside him. Since he has no origin at all, he consequently knows no end either—unless, absurdly, he once began to exist, in which case he would not be above all things but below what preceded him, found lesser in power because he is later in time. For this reason he is always immense, because nothing is greater than he is, and always eternal, because nothing is older than he is. What is without origin cannot be preceded by anything, since it has no time. Therefore he is immortal, not failing at the consummation's end. And because whatever is without origin is without law, he excludes the measure of time, since he recognizes himself as indebted to no one. Consequently, the human mind cannot worthily conceive what he is, how great he is, or what kind he is, nor can human eloquence express a virtue equal to his majesty. In contemplating and speaking of his majesty, all eloquence is rightly mute, and every mind is small. He is greater than mind itself, and cannot be thought as to how great he is, lest if he could be thought he would be less than the human mind that conceives him. He is also greater than all speech, and cannot be expressed, lest if he could be expressed he would be less than human speech, by which, when he is expressed, he can be encompassed and collected. For whatever is thought of him is less than he is, and whatever is spoken of him, compared with him, is less than he is. We can sense him in silence to some extent, but we cannot explain him in speech as he truly is. If you call him light, you have named a creature of his rather than him; you have not expressed him. If you call him virtue, you have named his power rather than him and set it forth. If you call him majesty, you have described his honor rather than him himself. Why should I make a long discussion, running through each thing individually? I will explain the whole matter once: whatever you say of him altogether, you have explained some thing of his, some virtue of his, rather than him. For what can you say or think worthily of him, who is greater than all speeches and all senses? Unless, in one way (and even this, how can we do it, how can we grasp it, how is it permitted to understand it?), we can apprehend what God is with our mind, if we think that he is that which cannot be understood as to its kind and magnitude, and cannot even enter into thought itself. For if the vision of our eyes is dulled by the sight of the sun, so that it cannot look at the orb itself, overcome by the brilliance of its rays, the same thing happens to the vision of the mind in every thought of God; and the more it strains to consider God, the more it is blinded by the light of its own thought. For what can you say worthily of him (to repeat once more), who is more sublime than all sublimity, higher than all height, deeper than all depth, more lucid than all light, clearer than all clarity, more splendid than all splendor, more robust than all robustness, more virile than all virtue, more beautiful than all beauty, truer than all truth, stronger than all strength, more majestic than all majesty, more powerful than all power, richer than all riches, more prudent than all prudence, more benign than all benignity, better than all goodness, more just than all justice, more merciful than all mercy? All kinds of virtues must be less than he who is both God and parent of all virtues, so that it can be truly said that he is God, who is such that nothing can be compared to him. He is above all that can be said. For he is a certain mind that generates and fills all things, which, without any beginning or end of time, moderates the causes of things—naturally linked for the utility of all—with supreme and perfect reason.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding God's immensity, eternity, and transcendence. Pass A provides a faithful rendering of the Latin, and Pass B maintains the nuance of the parenthetical interjections and the repetitive superlative structure. All clauses, including the conditional 'unless' clauses and the specific comparisons of attributes, are preserved.
